title: Chitrakoot
hook: you can still walk barefoot around the hill where the exiles lived

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chitrakoot, the bright mountain, a house of leaves, and Valmiki inside his own story. Did you notice your own front door? A new week begins, and today we visit Chitrakoot as it is now. Day five hundred forty.

Most stories happen in places you can't go. Nobody can buy a ticket to Middle-earth. But on the border of two Indian states, Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh, there's a small town called Chitrakoot, with a green hill, a river and a lot of temples. Every day, pilgrims arrive there, take off their shoes, and start walking. They're walking around the hill where, they believe, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana once lived in a hut of leaves.
screen: `PLACES YOU CAN'T GO.` → `A TOWN CALLED CHITRAKOOT.` → `PILGRIMS TAKE OFF THEIR SHOES.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Chitrakuta is made of two Sanskrit words: chitra, bright, wonderful, many-colored, and kuta, a peak. The bright peak. In Hindi it's usually said Chitrakoot. Valmiki names a river there too, the Mandakini, and today the Mandakini still runs through the town. Its main bathing place is called Ram Ghat, and in the evenings people float lamps on the water. The hill at the center of the pilgrimage is called Kamadgiri, often explained as the hill that grants wishes. Many devotees walk all the way around it barefoot, a circuit of a few miles, stopping at shrines along the path. Walking around something holy, keeping it on your right, is called parikrama, and it's one of the oldest ways Hindus honor a sacred place. There's another layer. Chitrakoot is also linked with the poet Tulsidas, who retold the Ramayana in Hindi in the 1500s. A well-known tradition says that Tulsidas, sitting at Ram Ghat, was granted a vision of Rama there. So the town carries two Ramayanas at once: Valmiki's Sanskrit and Tulsidas's Hindi. Here's why that matters for our reading. The Ramayana isn't only a book. For many Hindus, its places are real places, and walking them is a way of reading the story with your feet. Scholars debate which modern sites match which verses, and the text doesn't settle every question. But the pilgrims aren't waiting for scholars. Every morning they take off their shoes, and they walk.
screen: `CHITRA AND KUTA: THE BRIGHT PEAK.` · `THE MANDAKINI AND RAM GHAT.` · `KAMADGIRI AND THE PARIKRAMA.` · `TULSIDAS'S VISION AT RAM GHAT.` · then, large: `READING THE STORY WITH YOUR FEET.`

segments.voice: Sit, and imagine you're one of those pilgrims, standing at the foot of the green hill with your shoes in your hand. Feel the cool ground under your bare feet. Take one slow step in your mind with each breath: in, lift; out, place. Keep the hill on your right. You don't need to get anywhere. Just keep walking, one breath at a time. The bell holds the time.
Chitrakoot, today. A pilgrim town on the Mandakini, where people walk barefoot around Kamadgiri hill and read the Ramayana with their feet.
Your line: Chitrakoot. Today, take a short walk slowly, as if the ground you're on were part of a story. Day five hundred forty.

howItsDone: Pilgrims at Chitrakoot bathe at Ram Ghat on the Mandakini and walk the parikrama, the circuit around Kamadgiri hill, often barefoot, especially on new-moon days.

original.note: Sanskrit citrakūṭa: the bright or many-colored peak, citra plus kūṭa; Chitrakoot in Hindi.
